blocks.text: It is proved that תנשמת thinsemeth in Levit. XI, 30. is the chameleon.

In the passage we are dealing with, only תנשמת thinsemeth remains, that is, the mole, if we follow the Greeks and Jerome, and among the Chaldees Onkelos, and the Hebrews of recent times, Solomon, Kimchi, Pomarius, Aquinas; and the modern translators of the Bible, Pagninus, Münster, Arias, the Genevans, the English, the Italians, etc. Although the authority of all these carries great weight with me, two things above all keep it from drawing my assent, which I have already noted elsewhere. The first is that the mole was already dealt with in the preceding verse. For we have proved, with arguments that no one will easily refute ^{a)}, that it is חולד choled. Therefore תנשמת thinsemeth in this verse is something else, unless we wish Moses to have forbidden the same animal twice in one and the same sequence of text, and imagine him to have spoken thus: Among the creeping things that creep upon the earth, these shall be unclean to you: the mole, and the mouse, and the land crocodile, [col. 1079] etc. and the mole. Moreover, I do not see at all how the name תנשמת thinsemeth, which is derived from breath and breathing, can fit the mole, whose breathing is so slight [II, 504] that it spends whole days under the earth, as fish do under water. Hence the burrows of the mole and of the underground mouse are distinguished by this mark: when they are buried with earth, the mouse opens them at once so as not to suffocate, whereas the mole often unseals them only on the second or third day. Accordingly many of the ancients saw that תנשמת is not the mole; among them three other, very different, renderings of this word are found.
First, to the Samaritan translator תנשמת is [?], that is, the weasel, which in Chaldee is כרכושתא, and in Syriac ܟܒܟܘܫܬܐ, with the first radical doubled, whereas the Samaritans double the second.

Second, for the same word תנשמת the Syriac has ܝܘܕܥܝܕܐ jodaida, the many-footed one; and the Arabic manuscripts have البدال وهو أم اربعة اربعين [al-badāl wa-huwa umm arbaʿa arbaʿīn] Albedal, which is the mother of forty-four, supply feet; that is, which has 44 feet, i.e. the iulus or scolopendra. But for بدال [badāl] bedal, a meaningless word, one should read ندال [nadāl] nedal. For in Chaldee and among the Talmudists נדל nedal or nedel is the scolopendra. Thus below in verse 42, where among the creeping things of the earth כל מרבה רגלים is forbidden, whatever creeping thing has many feet, Gr. ὃ πολυπληθεῖ ποσὶν [ho polyplēthei posin], Jonathan has נדל דמסגי ריגלין, nedal, which is many-footed, that is, the scolopendra. And the Talmudists in Chullin ch. 3, fol. 67b: מרבה רגלים זה נדל, that which has many feet, that is, nedal. And there the Gloss: נדל מאה רגלים קורין לו, Nedal is commonly called the hundred-footed, a definite number, of course, for an indefinite one. But the Arabs, who usually speak precisely, call it the mother of 44 feet. Thus Avicenna, book 4, Fen 6, tract. 6, where he treats of small animals whose bite is venomous, in chapter 19 describes the animal الاربعة والاربعين [al-arbaʿa wa-l-arbaʿīn], that is, of forty-four feet, as follows: هو الحيوان المعروف بدخال الاذن وربما كان في طول شبر وله في كل جانب اثنان وعشرون قايمة وقد يمشي قدما وقد ينكص بحاله [huwa al-ḥayawān al-maʿrūf bi-dakhkhāl al-udhn wa-rubbamā kāna fī ṭūl shibr wa-lahu fī kull jānib ithnān wa-ʿishrūn qāyima wa-qad yamshī quduman wa-qad yankuṣu bi-ḥālihi] It is a well-known animal, because it enters the ear. Usually it is a span in length. On each side it has twenty-two feet, and it sometimes walks forward, sometimes moves backward. That the scolopendra enters the ear I have read nowhere else. But that it moves ἐπὶ τὴν οὐρὰν [epi tēn ouran], toward the tail, is said by the Philosopher, History, book 4, chapter 7. Hence Nicander, Theriaca verse 812, calls it ἀμφικαρὴς σκολόπενδρα [amphikarēs skolopendra]. On which words the Scholiast: Ἀμφικαρὴς δὲ, ἤγουν δικέφαλος. Ψευδῶς δέ φησιν, οὐ γάρ ἐστιν. Ἀλλ᾽, ὡς Ἀριστοτέλης φησὶν, εἰς τοὐπίσω πολλάκις ἕρπει, καὶ παρέχει δόξαν τοῦ δικέφαλος εἶναι [Amphikarēs de, ēgoun dikephalos. Pseudōs de phēsin, ou gar estin. All', hōs Aristotelēs phēsin, eis toupisō pollakis herpei, kai parechei doxan tou dikephalos einai]. As for the number of feet, different authors define it differently, so that it need not be the same in every place. However that may be, that the scolopendra is meant by this name is taught us by Abenbitar on the chapter of Dioscorides Περὶ σκολοπένδρας θαλασσίας [Peri skolopendras thalassias], whose name, after he has rendered it in Arabic letters thus, [II, 505] سقولوفندريا تالاسيا هو حيوان بحري وسمي باسم الحيوان الذي يقال له اربعة واربعون [sqūlūfandriyā tālāsiyā huwa ḥayawān baḥrī wa-summiya bi-ism al-ḥayawān alladhī yuqāl lahu arbaʿa wa-arbaʿūn] This is a sea animal, [col. 1080] which they call the 44-footed.
